study_material.title: Partnerships - Complete Study Notes
study_material.introduction: In partnership problems, profit is shared in proportion to capital multiplied by the time it stayed invested. Once you compute each partner's 'capital-months', every question reduces to dividing an amount in a ratio.
learning_objectives: Compute profit shares from capital and time
Handle partners joining or leaving mid-year
Deal with withdrawals and additional investments
Split profits when a working partner takes a salary or commission first

concepts.heading: 1. The Core Rule
concepts.body: Profit share is proportional to (capital x time). If A invests Ca for Ta months and B invests Cb for Tb months, shares are in ratio CaTa : CbTb. When times are equal it reduces to the capital ratio; when capitals are equal it reduces to the time ratio.

concepts.heading: 2. Partner Joining Later
concepts.body: A partner who joins after k months invests for (12 - k) months of the year. Compute capital-months for each partner over the same accounting period and form the ratio. Example: A puts 50,000 for 12 months, B joins after 4 months with 75,000: 600,000 vs 600,000 - equal shares.

concepts.heading: 3. Changing Capital
concepts.body: If a partner adds or withdraws money mid-way, break their timeline into segments and sum capital x months across segments. Example: 8,000 for 9 months then withdrawn entirely = 72,000 capital-months.

concepts.heading: 4. Working Partner Compensation
concepts.body: A working partner may receive a salary or a fixed percentage of profit first; only the remainder is split in the capital-month ratio. Always deduct the compensation before dividing.

formulas: Equal times: ratio = capitals; equal capitals: ratio = times
Remaining profit after salary/commission is split by capital-months
shortcut_methods: Work in thousands to keep numbers small
Simplify each capital-month product before forming the ratio
If shares are equal, capital-month products must be equal - use this to find unknown capital or joining time
common_mistakes: Ignoring the time dimension when a partner joins late
Splitting the whole profit when a working partner's cut must come first
Using months invested for one partner and years for another
study_material.summary: Convert every investment to capital-months, form the ratio, deduct any working-partner compensation first, then divide the profit.
quick_revision_notes: Joining after k months means 12-k months invested

solved_examples.question: A and B invest Rs. 30,000 and Rs. 40,000 in a business. Divide a profit of Rs. 14,000.
solved_examples.step_by_step: Ratio 3:4, total 7 parts; each part = 2,000. Shares 6,000 and 8,000.
solved_examples.shortcut: Same time invested, so ratio = capital ratio.

solved_examples.shortcut: Bigger capital for fewer months can exactly offset.

X invests Rs. 9,000. After 3 months Y joins with Rs. 12,000. The year-end profit is Rs. 39,000. Y's share is:
questions.explanation: X: 9000 x 12 = 108,000; Y: 12000 x 9 = 108,000. Equal capital-months, so Y gets half of 39,000 = 19,500.
